doc.title: Pug Horton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998

chapter: Growing up with jazz in northern England
title: Hearing Bessie Smith and Jelly Roll Morton in northern England
summary: Rowe asks when she wanted music; she was hooked by Bessie Smith's Back Water Blues and Jelly Roll Morton, never planning a career.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yes, an honorary doctorate, and Doctor Wilber will be receiving—
Yes. Don’t call him any Doc.

No Doc. That’s not quite complete. You’ve seen the music business from a number of sides as a performer yourself, and now as managing and getting in to the logistics of moving around the world in music. Was there a time in your youth when you said I really want to be in music? At what point did you think that that might be possibility?

Do you know I don’t think I ever planned my life to begin with. I wish I could say that I had made big plans. But what happened to me was I was a kid growing up in the north of England, and of course jazz is not indigenous to the north of England. And I heard a recording of Bessie Smith. And all I can say, Monk, is that I didn’t understand. If you remember on that “Back Water Blues” and she sings “when it rains five days/and the sky turns black as night” I didn’t even know, really, what she said. When it rains five days and the sky turns black as night. I’d never heard anything like it. It was like a riveting sound. And I knew that I wanted to do something that would bring me closer to learning more about what was going on there. I knew there was something very special happening. And then I listened to Jelly Roll Morton’s original “Jelly Roll Blues” and I got hooked on jazz. But I never really saw myself as being a part of it. I mean I just went with the flow, and I did everything that came along you know. And if it required sort of singing a song for some show or something, that’s what I’d do or I’d dance. And sort of to sing some chorus on “Ice Cream” or something like that you know, was kind of fun. And I became a devotee of jazz music, which was rather interesting because there were very few devotees of jazz music in north England.
